The idea

Better AI begins with
knowing its limits.

AI systems increasingly make predictions and decisions in situations where their knowledge is incomplete. Recognising these limits is essential to knowing when to rely on a prediction, seek more information, or reconsider a decision.

This ability to understand and reason about the limits of one's knowledge is what we call epistemic intelligence. The workshop connects philosophical, mathematical, and statistical foundations with the practical challenges of building AI that can learn and act reliably under uncertainty.

The EIML story

A growing conversation.

EIML began at EurIPS 2025 in Copenhagen, bringing together researchers interested in how machine learning can recognise and respond to gaps in its knowledge. The second edition, at ICML 2026 in Seoul, expanded the conversation to generative AI, robustness, safety, and continual learning. EIML3 continues this journey in Saarbrücken, connecting the foundations of imprecision and uncertainty with the needs of modern AI.

Topics

Three perspectives.
One shared question.

What does it take for AI to reason well when its knowledge is incomplete?

01

Philosophical foundations of imprecision and uncertainty

Reliable AI needs a clear account of what it means to know, to doubt, and to act with incomplete information. We explore how these ideas should shape the way AI systems represent and communicate the limits of their knowledge.

  • What does it mean for an AI system to know something or recognise its own ignorance?
  • When should uncertainty change a system's beliefs, explanations, or decisions?
02

Mathematical and statistical aspects of imprecision and uncertainty

When evidence is limited, a single precise probability may not fully express what is known. We study mathematical representations of incomplete knowledge and statistical methods for learning, prediction, and decisions under uncertainty.

  • How can we represent and measure uncertainty without claiming more precision than the evidence supports?
  • Which guarantees remain useful when data are scarce, assumptions fail, or conditions change?
03

Applications to modern AI

AI systems need to recognise unfamiliar situations and respond appropriately as their environment changes. We connect uncertainty research to robustness, generalisation, continual learning, and reliable decision-making in modern AI.

  • How can language models, generative systems, and AI agents recognise and communicate gaps in their knowledge?
  • When should a system seek information, revise what it has learned, defer to a person, or decline to act?

CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security

Join us at CISPA in beautiful Saarbrücken, a city on the River Saar where a lively research community meets old-town squares, riverside walks, and a distinctive Franco-German character.

Beyond the workshop, explore the cafés around St. Johanner Markt, the baroque Ludwigskirche, and the paths along the river.
